key_insight: CATTS (a simple test-time scaling scheme) dynamically allocates compute across steps of multi-step agents so that scarce inference budget targets high-risk steps, avoiding the diminishing returns of uniform scaling and reducing compounded errors over long horizons.
problem_solved: How to improve reliability and efficiency of agentic, multi-step models at inference: small per-step errors compound over long tasks, and naively increasing compute uniformly per step gives poor returns and wasted budget.
method: Empirically characterize per-step error/uncertainty patterns for multi-step web agents to identify where mistakes concentrate.
Dynamically reallocate inference compute (e.g., sampling, search, or repeated queries) to steps flagged as high-uncertainty or high-impact instead of uniformly scaling every step.
Use a budget-aware policy (thresholds or learned controller) to trade off overall compute and end-to-end task performance.
impact: CATTS improves end-to-end performance and reliability of long-horizon agents while using inference budget more efficiently, enabling practitioners to get better results without linearly increasing cost. It’s immediately applicable to production web agents and multi-step LM workflows.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing an agent executing multiple steps with variable-size compute bubbles (bigger bubbles on high-uncertainty steps) vs uniform bubbles for baseline.
Line chart comparing task success vs total inference compute for uniform scaling and CATTS (CATTS reaches higher success with same or less compute).
Heatmap or bar chart of per-step uncertainty/error rates, annotated to show where CATTS reallocates resources.
Budget-allocation infographic (pie or stacked bar) illustrating how compute is shifted from low-impact steps to high-impact steps under a fixed budget.
paper_authors: Nicholas Lee, Lutfi Eren Erdogan, Chris Joseph John, Surya Krishnapillai, Michael W. Mahoney
